Hook: In the summer of 2001 the United States Treasury began mailing tax rebate cheques: three hundred dollars to a single filer, six hundred to a couple, to about two-thirds of American households. There were too many to send at once. So they went out over ten weeks, from late July to late September, and the week in which a household's cheque was mailed was set by the second-to-last digit of its Social Security number. A zero went first, a nine went last.

That digit has nothing to do with a household's income, its needs or its plans. So the timing was random: an experiment that no one had designed. And the timing was announced. Every household could know when its cheque would come. The theory of the day, Milton Friedman's, says that money you know is coming is already in your spending plans. So the day it arrives should change nothing.

Here is what the national accounts saw, month by month, with June 2001 set to one hundred. Disposable income, after tax and in real terms, jumps in July, August and September, as the cheques go out. Spending on nondurable goods and services barely moves. The saving rate rises from 4.2 percent in June to 6.9 percent in September, and falls back in October. So did households simply save their cheques? The aggregate cannot say. Too much else happened that autumn, the attacks of September the eleventh among it. But the random timing can. Three economists, David Johnson, Jonathan Parker and Nicholas Souleles, compared households whose cheques came early with households whose cheques came late. The day of arrival mattered. How much, you'll guess in a moment.

This part's question: how do households decide how much to spend today? How should a household that looks ahead spread its income over its life? Why do real households spend windfalls faster than that theory says? And what does it mean for stimulus cheques, for pensions, and for how much a nation saves?
One card before we start. This part is about how saving is modelled and measured. Its households, pensions and windfalls are illustrations, not advice about anyone's money.
Economics, Built. Part twenty-two: consumption and saving.

This part continues Act Five. You'll meet Keynes's consumption function, the puzzle Simon Kuznets found in it, and Friedman's answer. You'll derive permanent income and the life cycle, and test Robert Hall's claim that consumption is a random walk on sixty years of American data. You'll solve a household's precautionary saving on a grid, read the rebate experiments, and meet households that are rich and still live hand to mouth. Then whether government debt is wealth, how generations trade with one another through pensions, and why China saves so much. And a dial on how much of a windfall people spend, the design of stimulus, and spending through unemployment.
PlayIt: Chapter one. Play it: what happened to the cheques?

Your turn. A household's rebate arrives in the week its digit says. Of each dollar, how much did it spend on nondurable goods and services, in the three months the cheque arrived? Nondurables as the survey counts them: food, fuel, utilities, clothes, health, entertainment. Not cars or furniture. A, two cents; B, twenty-five cents; C, fifty cents; or D, ninety cents. Pause, and choose.

And one more number to hold on to, about you this time. An unexpected payment equal to a month of your income arrives today. How much of it would you spend in the next three months? Write it down. Chapter ten compares it with what thousands of people told surveys, and with what lottery winners actually did.

Here are the answers, with your four choices marked as dashed lines. Friedman's theory says a household should spread a windfall over the rest of its life. At an interest rate of three percent that is under one cent of each dollar a quarter. Johnson, Parker and Souleles found that households spent twenty to forty cents of each rebate dollar on nondurables in the three months it arrived, and more in the three months after. If you chose B, you were right. In 2008 a second round of payments, again timed by Social Security numbers, gave twelve to thirty cents on nondurables. And counting what people spent on cars and other durable goods, fifty to ninety cents. If you chose D thinking of a new car, that is not far off either. Either way, the theory of the day missed by a factor of twenty or more.
Keynes: Chapter two. Keynes's function and Kuznets's puzzle.

In 1936 John Maynard Keynes stated what he called a fundamental psychological law. Men are disposed, as a rule and on the average, to increase their consumption as their income increases, but not by as much as the increase in their income. Write it as a line: consumption equals a constant plus a fraction b of income, with b between zero and one. That fraction is the marginal propensity to consume. Because of the constant, the average propensity, consumption over income, falls as income rises. The rich save a larger share. And household surveys agreed: across families in any one year, saving rises with income.

Then the puzzle. In 1946 Simon Kuznets assembled American national income back to 1869. Income per head had risen several times over. The share of it consumed had hardly moved, decade after decade. The modern accounts say the same. Since 1959 real disposable income has risen about 7.5 times, and consumption has stayed between 0.82 and 0.94 of it. Keynes's function, fitted across families, says the ratio should fall as a country grows richer. It does not. Across households the rich save more; across time the nation saves the same share. Both are true. Why?

The Island can show you, because its households now number 10,000, and we know their truth. Here is a survey of them in one year: each household's measured income, and what it consumed. Fit Keynes's line through them: a constant of 0.31 and a slope of 0.62. And by tenths of income, the poorest tenth consumes 1.27 times its income this year, more than it earns, and the richest 0.72. The rich save more. Keynes's function, found again.

But we planted something else. Every household on the Island consumes nine tenths of its permanent income, the income it expects to earn on average. Its measured income this year adds a transitory part: a good harvest, a bad one. There is no Keynesian constant, and no rich household saves a larger share of its permanent income. A household with a good year looks rich in the survey and seems to save. One with a bad year looks poor and seems to borrow. Sorting by this year's income sorts by luck. That is Milton Friedman's answer to Kuznets, in 1957: an errors-in-variables problem, from Part 4. The slope in logs is the share of the variance of income that is permanent, here 0.74. The survey gives 0.73. And as everyone's permanent income grows for 60 years, the ratio of consumption to income stays at nine tenths, as Kuznets found.
PIH: Chapter three. Permanent income and the life cycle.

Both answers start from Part seven's Euler equation. A household choosing how much to consume today and tomorrow sets the marginal utility of a dollar spent today equal to the discounted marginal utility of what that dollar becomes tomorrow, one plus r of it, valued at beta. At the best plan there is no gain from shifting a dollar either way. If patience just offsets the interest rate, beta times one plus r equals one, and with marginal utility falling in consumption, the plan is flat: expected consumption tomorrow equals consumption today. The household smooths.

Now add the budget. The present value of everything the household will consume equals what it owns today plus the present value of everything it expects to earn, its human wealth. With a flat plan and a long horizon, consumption is the interest on total wealth: r over one plus r, times assets plus human wealth. Friedman called that permanent income. So a windfall of one dollar, once, raises consumption by r over one plus r: at three percent, 2.9 cents a year, for ever. Under one cent a quarter. That was the answer the theory gave in the game. A raise of a dollar a year, for good, raises human wealth by one plus r over r dollars, and consumption by the whole dollar. And a change that was foreseen, like a cheque whose date was announced, is already in the plan. Only news moves consumption.

Franco Modigliani and Richard Brumberg, in 1954, gave the same logic a lifetime with an end. Income rises through a working life, peaks, and stops at retirement. Consumption, by the Euler equation, stays flat. The gap is saving, so wealth follows a hump: built up while working, it peaks at retirement, at 65 here, at about 14 years of average income, and is run down to nothing by the end. The young save, the old dissave.

The life cycle says something about nations, too. Saving comes from the young and dissaving from the old. If income grows quickly, each young generation is richer than the old one was, its saving outweighs the old's dissaving, and the nation saves more. If the population ages, more retirees are running down their wealth, and the nation saves less. No psychological law is needed. A country's saving rate depends on its growth and its age structure, which is why it was stable while America's growth was. Modigliani's Nobel prize, in 1985, was for his analyses of saving and of financial markets.
Hall: In 1978 Robert Hall turned the Euler equation into a prediction anyone could test. If the household plans so that it expects tomorrow's consumption to equal today's, then whatever it actually consumes tomorrow differs from today only by a surprise, an error with mean zero given everything known today. Consumption is a random walk. Its change is news, and news cannot be forecast. So nothing known today, not past income, not a cheque whose date was announced, should predict how consumption changes next. You don't need to know the household's income process, its wealth or its preferences to test that. You only need a regression. Hall's own test, on post-war American data, found that lagged income added nothing. Lagged stock prices did help, a little.

So run it. Take sixty years of American quarters, from 1960 to the end of 2019, before the pandemic's swings. Consumption here is real spending on nondurable goods and services, the part of spending that is used up as it is bought. Income is real disposable income. Regress the growth of consumption on the growth of income two, three and four quarters earlier. Hall says every coefficient is zero. They are 0.09, 0.10 and 0.05, each with a standard error of about 0.03. Together, an F statistic of 6.8, against a one percent critical value of 3.9. Income growth from six months to a year ago predicts consumption growth today. Some of the income households could see coming, they spent only when it came.

One detail matters here, and it is the kind that trips up careful people. Why leave out last quarter's income? Because the data are averages. The national accounts report spending over each quarter, not at an instant, and the average of a random walk over a quarter has changes that are correlated with each other. Averaging three months, the correlation of successive changes is 0.21, with no failure of the theory at all. Holbrook Working pointed this out in 1960. Any variable from the quarter just before shares in that artefact, so a clean test starts at the second lag. In the data the correlation is 0.47, more than averaging can explain: spending itself moves more slowly than a random walk.
Sensitivity: Chapter five. Too sensitive, and too smooth.

Hall's test failed in the direction Marjorie Flavin had already found in 1981: consumption responds to changes in income that could have been predicted. Economists call it excess sensitivity. In 1989 John Campbell and Gregory Mankiw gave it a size. Suppose there are two kinds of household. A share lambda of income goes to households who follow a rule of thumb: they spend what they get, when they get it. The rest goes to Hall's households, whose consumption moves only with news. You cannot estimate lambda by regressing consumption growth on income growth, because the news that moves Hall's households also moves income. Use instead the part of income growth that was predictable two quarters earlier: an instrument, in the sense of Part four.

First on the Island, where we know the answer. We plant lambda at 0.4: four tenths of income goes to households who spend what they get. Then we run two hundred island economies for sixty years of quarters each. Ordinary least squares, economy by economy, averages 0.67. The news contaminates it. Instrumenting with income growth two quarters earlier, the estimates centre on the truth, a median of 0.38. But they are wide. Sixty years of quarters is not much data, and the instrument predicts income growth only modestly.

Now on the real thing. On American quarters from 1960 to 2019, least squares gives 0.23. Instrumenting with income and consumption growth two to four quarters earlier gives 0.65, with a standard error of 0.13. But the first stage is weak, an F of 4.2, far below the rule of thumb of ten, and Part four showed what weak instruments do: they pull the estimate toward least squares and make its standard error too small. Read the number loosely. Campbell and Mankiw's own estimates, on data to the mid-1980s, were about one half. Whatever the exact number, a large share of income, not a rounding error, goes to households who spend it when it comes.

Then the opposite failure. In American data, income growth is persistent: a good year tends to be followed by another, an autocorrelation of about 0.23 in annual growth. If so, a surprise in income raises permanent income by more than it raises this year's income, and a permanent-income household should change its consumption by more than its income changed. Income growth has a standard deviation of 1.6 percent a year. The theory predicts consumption growth with a standard deviation of 2.0. Actual spending on nondurables and services: 1.3. Consumption is too smooth. Angus Deaton called it a paradox in 1987. John Campbell and Deaton then showed that excess smoothness and excess sensitivity are the same failure seen two ways: consumption responds too little to news when it arrives and catches up later, when the news has become predictable.

So consumption is smoother than income, though not as smooth as the theory first said. It goes on the series' list of facts. Quarter by quarter from 1960 to 2019, American spending on nondurables and services grew with a standard deviation of 0.44 percent, income with 0.87. Agora's column is filled by the households of the next chapter, who smooth, but not completely.
Buffer: Chapter six. Precautionary saving and the buffer stock.

Hall's households have no reason to fear risk in what they spend. To get his random walk exactly, he gave them quadratic utility, whose marginal utility is a straight line. Real marginal utility curves. Here it falls with consumption as one over c squared. If consumption tomorrow is a sure one, a dollar tomorrow is worth one. If it is half or one and a half with equal chances, the average marginal utility is 2.22: the bad state's high value outweighs the good state's low one. Risk raises the value of a dollar saved, so a household with a convex marginal utility saves more when its income is uncertain. Miles Kimball called that curvature prudence. Its saving is precautionary: a buffer against bad years.

Stephen Zeldes showed in 1989 that prudence bends the consumption function. Angus Deaton and Christopher Carroll built the household that bears its name. Income is a permanent part, which grows and takes permanent shocks, times a transitory part. The shocks have a spread of about ten percent each, and there is a small chance, half a percent a year, of no income at all: a lost job, an illness. The household cannot borrow, and it is impatient: with its income rising, it would like to borrow against the future if it could. Measure everything relative to permanent income. Cash on hand, m, is what it has to spend this year. The Euler equation now has an expectation over next year's shocks, and next year's cash depends on what it saves. These are the Island's planted parameters.

How do you solve it? The obvious way, for each level of cash, searches for the consumption that satisfies the Euler equation, a root found again and again. In 2006 Carroll found a shortcut, the endogenous grid method. Fix a grid, not of cash, but of what the household carries forward. For each amount carried forward, next year's cash is known in every state, so the right side of the Euler equation is just an average. Invert marginal utility to get the consumption that makes the equation hold, and add it to what was carried forward: that is the cash the household must have had. The pairs of cash and consumption are the new consumption function. Repeat until it stops changing. No equation solved numerically. Here it takes 133 rounds and a fraction of a second. Part fifty-two solves economies of a hundred thousand such households this way.

Here is the answer. Cash on hand, in years of permanent income, along the bottom. Consumption up the side. Without income risk, the impatient household spends everything it has until its cash passes a year's income, and then saves only a little: the blue line. With risk, the green line: it holds back at every level of cash, and the line bends. That bend is Zeldes's point. Where the line is steep, at low cash, an extra dollar is mostly spent: 0.89 of it at half a year's income, 0.57 at a year's. Where it is flat, among households with a cushion, almost none: 0.07 at five years. And there is a target, cash of about 1.43 years of income, where impatience, which pulls the stock down, just balances prudence, which builds it up. A household below the target saves toward it; one above spends down. The buffer stock.

Now give the Island twenty thousand such households, and let them live long enough that their cash settles into its long-run spread. The shaded hills show where they sit: most near the target, some below after bad years. The green line is the share of a windfall worth a month's income that each would spend within the year. Averaged over the Island, 0.23. For the tenth of households with the least cash, 0.38; for the tenth with the most, 0.16. The permanent-income household would spend 0.029. Prudence and impatience together give a propensity to spend eight times larger, and far larger for those short of cash. It is still below what the rebates showed in a single quarter. Keep that gap in mind.
HandToMouth: The rebates hit hardest where liquid wealth was low. But which households are those? Wealth comes in two kinds. Liquid wealth is cash and bank accounts, ready to spend. Illiquid wealth is a house or a retirement account. Illiquid wealth pays more: the rent you no longer pay, the tax breaks, an employer's matching contribution. But it is costly to reach. You cannot spend a bedroom. Call a household hand-to-mouth if it has little or no liquid wealth on payday. Greg Kaplan, Giovanni Violante and Justin Weidner counted them in 2014: about a third of American households. And over two-thirds of those were not poor. They owned a house or a pension. They are the wealthy hand-to-mouth, and they spend a windfall as fast as the poor do.

The Island can show the mechanism with a shortcut. Sixty percent of its households own illiquid wealth, about three years of income at the median, earning seven percent a year against three on cash. For an owner, every dollar kept in cash gives up the higher return. So on its cash, an owner discounts as if it were less patient: a beta of 0.924 instead of 0.96. It keeps less cash, and lives closer to the steep part of the consumption function. Renters solve chapter six's problem unchanged. Kaplan and Violante's own model has two assets and a cost of moving between them; this is the part of it that matters here.

Here are the Island's households, each a dot: net worth along the bottom, on a log scale, and the share of a month's windfall it would spend within the year. Owners in purple, renters in yellow. The owners are far richer: a median net worth of 3.3 years of income against 0.44. And they spend more of a windfall, 0.36 against 0.23. Across all households, the share spent rises with net worth: a correlation of +0.48. Richer households spending faster looks like a contradiction. Now move every dot to its liquid wealth instead. They fall onto a single curve. The correlation is -0.97. What a household spends out of a windfall depends on the cash it has, not on what it owns.
Ricardo: The 2001 rebate was a tax cut paid for by borrowing. Does that make households richer? Suppose the government cuts taxes today by a month's income and borrows to pay for it. Twenty years later it must repay the debt with interest: at three percent, a tax of 0.151 of a year's income. Discount that later tax back to today and it is exactly the cut. The household that will pay the later tax is no richer. A permanent-income household therefore saves the whole cut, ready for the tax. Private saving rises one for one with public borrowing, and national saving does not change. Robert Barro made the argument rigorous in 1974, and David Ricardo had stated it, and doubted it, in 1820. Hence the name: Ricardian equivalence. Borrowing and taxing are equivalent.

It is a benchmark, and its value is in showing exactly what has to fail for deficits to matter. First, liquidity. A household short of cash spends the cut now, whatever it will owe later, because it would have liked to borrow anyway. Second, lives end. If the tax will fall on the next generation, this one is richer, and spends. Barro's reply: parents who care about their children will save the cut and leave it to them, to pay the tax. That needs bequests to be operative, which is a question about real families. Third, real taxes distort, no one knows who will pay them, and people may simply not be paying attention. And the cleanest test is the 2001 rebate itself, a cut financed by borrowing. Households spent twenty to forty percent of it in a single quarter.

On the Island, the same debt-financed cut lands on four kinds of household. The Ricardian household spends none of it. A buffer-stock renter spends 0.23 of it within the year. The Island as a whole, owners and renters together, 0.31. And households short of cash, 0.45. What is spent is what national saving loses. So whether government borrowing crowds out saving, and whether a tax cut stimulates, depends on who gets the cut. Part thirty-two, on the Treasury, comes back to it.
OLG: Everything so far has been one household and its own life. But lives overlap. In 1958 Paul Samuelson imagined the simplest economy with that feature. Each generation lives two periods: young and working, then old and retired. Goods cannot be stored, so the old have nothing. The young cannot lend to the old, because the old will be gone before they could repay. Without some arrangement, the old starve. The arrangement is money. Each old generation holds pieces of paper, and sells them to the young for goods. The young accept the paper because the next young generation will accept it from them. If each generation is larger than the last, the paper buys more when they are old: its return is the growth of the population, 1.4 a generation here, about 1.1 percent a year. A pay-as-you-go pension, in which today's workers pay today's retirees, is the same contract, written by the state. Samuelson called it a social contrivance.

In 1965 Peter Diamond put capital into Samuelson's economy. Now the young earn a wage, consume part of it, and save the rest. Their savings become next period's capital, spread over the next, larger, generation of workers. So capital per worker tomorrow is a function of capital per worker today, through the wage it pays the young. The old live on the return to their capital. Follow the map from a low start and it climbs to a steady state where the curve crosses the diagonal, here at 1.23.

Now the question that made Diamond's model famous. In Part twenty, Phelps's golden rule chose the capital stock that maximizes consumption in the steady state. Here it is where the return on capital equals the growth factor, one plus n. Take a patient economy, with beta 0.9 a generation. It saves so much that the return on capital, 1.27 a generation, is below the growth factor of 1.4. It has more capital than the golden rule. Every generation could consume more, now and for ever, if it had less. That is dynamic inefficiency, and it is a failure of competitive markets with no externality in sight. Introduce a pay-as-you-go pension. Each young worker pays d, each retiree receives the larger young generation's payments. It returns one plus n, more than capital, so the young save less, capital falls toward the golden rule, and every generation gains, up to a pension of 0.4. A free lunch, though a small one. In an impatient economy, beta 0.3, the return on capital is 2.60, above the growth factor. Now the pension pays less than the capital it displaces, and every size of pension lowers welfare: by 14 percent of consumption at the largest.

Which economy do we live in? The safe interest rate has often been below the growth rate, which looks like inefficiency. But with risk, comparing the safe rate with growth is misleading. In 1989 Andrew Abel, Gregory Mankiw, Lawrence Summers and Richard Zeckhauser gave a test that works with risk. Compare the cash that capital pays out, profits and rents, with the investment it absorbs. If capital pays out more than it takes in, year after year, the economy is efficient. In the United States and the other large OECD economies, it did. So a pay-as-you-go pension is a transfer between generations, not a free lunch. And switching to a funded system has a catch: the generation in between must pay for its parents' pensions and save for its own. Part forty-two takes that up.
China: Chapter twelve. The rich, bequests, and China.

Two pieces are still missing from the life cycle: the rich, and what people leave behind. Friedman's answer to Keynes said the rich only seem to save more, because a good year makes a household look rich. In 2004 Karen Dynan, Jonathan Skinner and Stephen Zeldes measured lifetime income more carefully, with education and income in other years, and found that saving rates rise with lifetime income too. So Friedman explained part of Keynes's cross-section, not all of it. Why would the lifetime rich save more? To leave bequests; because, as Christopher Carroll put it, wealth itself brings status and power, a capitalist spirit; and to guard against the costs of a long old age. How much of a nation's wealth is inherited rather than saved over a life? Laurence Kotlikoff and Lawrence Summers put it at about four-fifths in 1981; Modigliani, in 1988, at about a fifth. Much of the gap is about definitions, what counts as a transfer and how it grows, and it is still open.

Now the largest saving puzzle of our time. Here is household consumption as a share of output, from the Penn World Table, for six economies. In the United States it rose to about 0.69. In China it was 0.49 in 1990 and fell to 0.35 by 2010, recovering only to 0.41. Chinese households consumed about half as large a share of output as American households. Part of that is that households received a smaller share of income, as firms and the state saved too. But Chinese households also saved a very large share of what they received.

Why? Each explanation comes from this part. The life cycle: when income grows fast, the young who save are much richer than the old who dissave, and the one-child policy left fewer children to support parents in old age. Franco Modigliani and Shi Larry Cao made that case in 2004. Precaution: the reforms of the 1990s ended the iron rice bowl of state jobs, housing, health care and pensions. Marcos Chamon and Eswar Prasad found that urban households of all ages saved more as housing, schooling and health became private costs. And competition. As the ratio of boys to girls rose, parents of sons saved to improve their sons' chances in the marriage market, and the pressure spilled over to other households. Shang-Jin Wei and Xiaobo Zhang estimated that this competitive saving accounts for about half of the rise in household saving from 1990 to 2007, an estimate from their own work. Each has evidence. How the shares divide is argued.
Dials: Chapter thirteen. The Dials: the propensity to spend a windfall.

This part opens a dial: the propensity to spend a windfall, the share of a one-off payment that is spent soon after it arrives. The 2001 rebates: thirty percent, the middle of twenty to forty, on nondurables within the quarter. The 2008 payments: about twenty-one, the middle of twelve to thirty, before counting cars. The 2020 payments: about 10. Alaska's dividend, in account data: 25. Italians asked directly, over a year: 48. And the Island's buffer-stock households, a model, over a year: 23. The status: it depends on the setting. Who receives the money matters more than any average: households short of cash spend far more, whatever their net worth, and when many households already have cash, as in 2020, the share falls.

Put the dial next to the theory. Permanent income says about one percent a quarter. The one-asset buffer stock says about a quarter of a windfall within a year, and less within a quarter. The data say ten to forty percent within a quarter, on nondurables alone. The model with two assets, a house or pension that pays well and cash that does not, closes most of the gap, because it makes many households wealthy and short of cash at once. Kaplan and Violante built it to match the rebates. Part fifty-two builds whole economies of such households, and asks what they change about monetary and fiscal policy.
Practice: Chapter fourteen. In practice: stimulus and pensions.

What do governments do with all this? Start with stimulus. First, aim the money at households short of cash. They spend it; households with a cushion mostly save it. Second, speed. In 2020 the first payments went straight into the bank accounts the tax authority already had on file, within weeks. Third, the form. In 2008 Americans got one-time payments; in 2009 most workers got a tax credit as slightly lower withholding in every paycheque. Claudia Sahm, Matthew Shapiro and Joel Slemrod asked households in the Michigan survey what they did. Twenty-five percent said they would mostly spend the 2008 payment; thirteen percent said so of the 2009 paycheque increase. The same money, delivered differently, about half the response. And the tools for knowing all this are the ones in this part: random timing, account data, careful surveys.

Then pensions. A pay-as-you-go system, chapter eleven's, has today's workers pay today's retirees. A funded one has each generation save for itself. Either way, a life-cycle household should save the right amount whatever form the paperwork takes. It does not. Brigitte Madrian and Dennis Shea studied an American firm that, in 1998, switched its retirement plan from opt in to opt out. Among new hires, participation went from 37 percent to 86. And 76 percent of those enrolled automatically kept the default contribution rate of 3 percent, low as it was. Defaults are policy. The United Kingdom made automatic enrolment national from 2012; Part forty-two takes up pensions in full.

Who uses this? Treasuries and finance ministries, to design stimulus and to estimate what a tax change will do. Central banks, whose models need to know how spending responds to interest rates and income. Pension funds and their regulators, who choose defaults and contribution rates. And banks and financial technology firms, whose account data now let researchers see spending day by day, as Kueng's did, and as the frontier does.
Frontier: Chapter fifteen. Frontier: spending through unemployment.

The frontier is in bank accounts. Peter Ganong and Pascal Noel followed the accounts of people who lost their jobs and drew unemployment benefits, month by month. When the job is lost, nondurable spending drops about six percent. While benefits last, it drifts down by less than one percent a month. And when the benefits run out, on a date everyone knew from the start, spending drops about 12 percent, more than in all the months before combined. A permanent-income household would have seen that date coming and cut back early, spreading the loss. These households did not.

What it means. A drop in income that could be foreseen moved spending when it came: Hall's test, failed again, in data far better than any survey. For social insurance, Ganong and Noel calculate that making benefits last longer would smooth spending about four times as much as making them larger. For macroeconomics, it means models in which it matters who holds the cash. Greg Kaplan, Benjamin Moll and Giovanni Violante's heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian model, HANK, showed in 2018 that monetary policy then works less through interest rates on saving and more through jobs and incomes. Part fifty-two builds such economies, using the endogenous grid method of chapter six.

Open questions. Why the gap between theory and data: a shortage of cash, inattention, or the bother of planning, which Kueng's high earners suggest? Present bias: do people plan to save and then not, as Part forty-five will ask? Who saves for whom: bequests, families, and the state. And what the new data, from accounts, cards and payrolls, will show, day by day.
